title: The Constitution Has Clauses Courts Won't Touch
hook: Not every line in the Constitution gets fought over in court. Some, like the ban on quartering soldiers, have sat almost untouched for over two centuries — by choice, not by accident.
key_points: The 13th Amendment bans involuntary servitude except 'as a punishment for crime' — but in Kozminski (1988) the Supreme Court narrowed the clause to cover only physical or legal coercion, not psychological pressure, limiting its practical reach without ever fully defining it.

The Guarantee Clause (Article IV, Section 4) promises every state 'a Republican Form of Government' — since Luther v. Borden (1849), the Court has treated Guarantee Clause claims as a 'political question,' meaning it refuses to rule on them at all.

Even in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), on partisan gerrymandering, Chief Justice Roberts said the Guarantee Clause was arguably the more fitting basis for the claim — then dismissed it as nonjusticiable anyway.

The Third Amendment bars quartering soldiers in homes without consent; the Supreme Court has never ruled on its scope directly, citing it only as supporting evidence for privacy rights in cases like Griswold v. Connecticut (1965).

A federal appeals court (Engblom v. Carey, 1982) was the first to seriously apply the Third Amendment on its own terms — showing that a constitutional right can go essentially untested by the nation's highest court for two centuries.
content_html: Not every part of the Constitution gets a robust body of Supreme Court case law. Some provisions have sat almost untouched for centuries — and that's a choice the Court has made repeatedly, not an accident of history.
extra_html: Writing for SCOTUSblog, Nora Collins traces three examples. The 13th Amendment bars involuntary servitude except as criminal punishment, but in Kozminski (1988) the Court narrowed the clause to cover only physical or legal coercion — not psychological pressure — shrinking its reach without ever fully defining its outer limits. The Guarantee Clause promises every state "a Republican Form of Government," but since Luther v. Borden (1849) the Court has treated Guarantee Clause claims as a "political question" it won't rule on at all; even in 2019's Rucho v. Common Cause, on partisan gerrymandering, Chief Justice Roberts acknowledged the clause was arguably the more fitting basis for the claim, then dismissed it as nonjusticiable anyway. And the Third Amendment's ban on quartering soldiers in private homes has essentially never been directly interpreted by the Supreme Court — it shows up mainly as supporting evidence for privacy rights in cases like Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), while a federal appeals court, not the Supreme Court, first seriously applied it on its own terms in 1982. Together, the three cases make a point worth sitting with: a right or structural guarantee can be written plainly into the Constitution's text and still go essentially untested by the nation's highest court for generations. related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
related.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean for the Supreme Court to treat a constitutional claim as a 'political question'?
flashcards.back_html: The Court refuses to rule on the merits at all, treating the issue as belonging to the elected branches rather than the judiciary — used for Guarantee Clause claims since 1849.

flashcards.prompt: What happened to the Guarantee Clause argument in Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the partisan gerrymandering case?

choices.text: Chief Justice Roberts called it the more fitting basis for the claim, then dismissed it as nonjusticiable anyway
The Court ruled the Guarantee Clause directly bans partisan gerrymandering
The Court struck down the Guarantee Clause as unconstitutional

flashcards.explanation_html: Roberts acknowledged the clause's relevance but still applied the political-question doctrine to avoid deciding the underlying issue.

flashcards.prompt: How has the Supreme Court treated the Third Amendment's ban on quartering soldiers in private homes?

choices.text: It has never ruled on the amendment's scope directly, citing it only as supporting evidence in privacy-rights cases
It struck the amendment down as obsolete in the 20th century
It has issued several major rulings defining exactly what 'quartering' means

flashcards.explanation_html: The amendment has mostly appeared as a supporting citation, not as the direct subject of a ruling — a federal appeals court, not the Supreme Court, first applied it literally in 1982.
